axiom_nodes.title: Remarkably Early Historical Information for the Resurrection of Jesus - Gary Habermas
axiom_nodes.summary: A historical-apologetics lecture arguing from critically-accepted dating that the earliest Christian message (homologia) and pre-Pauline creeds about Jesus' death and resurrection originated in Jerusalem within one to two years of the cross, that Paul was converted within two to three years and verified his gospel with the eyewitnesses Peter and James, and that this early eyewitness chain rules out legendary development. The paper engages the canon mainly at the level of evidential/historical scaffolding for the resurrection and the reliability of early testimony; it does not state or derive the formal axiom system, though it touches the terminal-observer/BC family and the grace-versus-works distinction in passing.

axiom_nodes.name: BC1 — Terminal Observer Exists
axiom_nodes.notes: The lecture's whole argument presupposes a risen, self-authenticating Jesus as the terminal witness behind the early testimony, but it never frames this as the BC1 terminal-observer requirement.

axiom_nodes.name: BC5 — Superposition Preserved Until Collapse
axiom_nodes.notes: Habermas argues the resurrection data is too early to be myth, i.e., the tradition was not allowed to drift before being fixed by eyewitnesses; this is a historical analogue to preserving content until an authoritative observer fixes it, but no quantum claim is made.

axiom_nodes.name: BC7 — Information Conservation
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: But it keeps phone tag from being true.
axiom_nodes.notes: The core historical claim is that the original apostolic testimony was conserved intact through Paul's direct verification with Peter and James, ruling out lossy transmission.

axiom_nodes.name: BC8 — Voluntary Coupling
axiom_nodes.notes: The martyrdoms of Paul, Peter, and James are cited as evidence of sincerity, which is adjacent to voluntary coupling, but the lecture does not develop a coupling axiom.

axiom_nodes.name: A9.1 — External Intervention Required
axiom_nodes.notes: Paul's conversion is presented as an external encounter ('He meets Jesus') that reverses his prior hostility, but the lecture does not state an axiom of required external intervention.

axiom_nodes.name: C8.2 — Works Salvation Impossible
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: Good works will not get you in heaven.
axiom_nodes.notes: Explicitly asserted in the closing application, with the qualification that post-salvation works determine reward capacity.

axiom_nodes.name: P9.2 — Voluntary Coupling Preserved
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: In the New Testament the word believe means to jump in with both feet.
axiom_nodes.notes: Habermas insists NT belief is trust/surrender rather than mere assent, preserving a voluntary, non-coerced response; he explicitly denies this makes salvation by works.

axiom_nodes.name: P9.5 — Grace Available To All
axiom_nodes.notes: The gospel is presented as universally offered and universally preached, but the lecture does not formulate an availability axiom.

axiom_nodes.name: P10.1 — Soul Continuity
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: If you'll ever be eternal in the future, you're eternal now.
axiom_nodes.notes: Eternal life is said to begin in this life and continue into eternity, implying continuity of the person across death.

axiom_nodes.name: P10.2 — Soul Identity Persistence
axiom_nodes.notes: The claim that believers 'belong to the Lord' and leave with their king for eternity assumes personal persistence, but identity persistence is not argued.

axiom_nodes.name: T12.1 — Heaven As High-Phi Attractor
axiom_nodes.notes: Heaven and eternal reward are discussed in ordinary theological terms, not as a coherence attractor state.

axiom_nodes.name: T12.2 — Hell As Low-Phi Attractor
axiom_nodes.notes: The alternative to salvation is implied ('if not, you're not') but never characterized as a low-coherence attractor.

axiom_nodes.name: T16.1 — Christianity 8 of 8 BCs
axiom_nodes.notes: Habermas argues Christianity is uniquely vindicated by the resurrection data, which is structurally parallel to the 8-of-8 BC claim, but he never invokes the BC framework.

axiom_nodes.name: T16.6 — Atheism Fails BC1-BC6
axiom_nodes.notes: Atheist and agnostic scholars are cited as conceding the historical data yet not believing, which Habermas attributes to worldview rather than evidence; this is adjacent to but not the BC1-BC6 failure claim.

axiom_nodes.name: EV15.1 — Biblical Prophecy Validation
axiom_nodes.evidence_quote: How that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures, he was buried, rose again the third day according to the scriptures and appeared.
axiom_nodes.notes: The creedal formula is quoted as grounding the resurrection in the scriptures, functioning as scriptural validation of the event.

axiom_nodes.name: BRIDGE-PHY-THEO - Physics-Theology Bridge
axiom_nodes.notes: The lecture is purely historical-theological; it makes no physics bridge, though it supplies evidence the canon's bridge would need to accommodate.

axiom_nodes.name: PERSONHOOD — Agency, Intentionality, Relational Capacity
axiom_nodes.notes: Belief is characterized as personal trust, surrender, and covenant commitment ('I do'), presupposing agency, intentionality, and relational capacity.

atoms.title: Remarkably Early Historical Information for the Resurrection of Jesus - Gary Habermas
atoms.summary: Habermas argues that early, critically-accepted data (homologia, pre-Pauline creeds, Paul's conversion, and Paul's Jerusalem consultations with Peter and James) establish eyewitness testimony to the resurrection within 2-6 years of the cross, defeating 'telephone tag' myth objections. He also distinguishes factual from emotional doubt and closes with exhortation from 1 Cor 15:58.

atoms.name: Resurrection is Christianity's load-bearing claim
atoms.statementTechnical: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true; all other doctrinal disputes are non-fundamental.
atoms.statementPlain: If Jesus rose, Christianity is true; you don't have to solve every Bible problem.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that Jesus did not rise (e.g., tomb not empty / body produced) would falsify Christianity on this axiom.

atoms.name: Homologia: earliest agreed-upon gospel data
atoms.statementTechnical: The earliest agreed-upon data (homologia) in the early church centered on Jesus' deity, death, and resurrection, preached immediately after the crucifixion.
atoms.statementPlain: The first Christians' earliest agreed message was the death and resurrection of Jesus, preached right away.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that earliest Christian preaching centered on other topics, or that resurrection preaching began decades later, would falsify.

atoms.name: Pre-Pauline creeds date within 1-2 years of the cross
atoms.statementTechnical: Early creedal formulations (memorizable summaries of the homologia) originated in Jerusalem within 1-2 years of the crucifixion, likely from the apostles, and Paul probably knew them all.
atoms.statementPlain: The earliest Christian creeds came from Jerusalem within a year or two of Jesus' death, from the apostles themselves.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that the creeds postdate Paul or originate outside Jerusalem/apostolic circles would falsify.

atoms.name: Paul's conversion within 2-3 years of the cross
atoms.statementTechnical: Paul was converted approximately 2-3 years after the crucifixion, an event granted by critical scholars, giving an eyewitness link to the earliest data.
atoms.statementPlain: Paul became a Christian just two or three years after Jesus died.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Evidence that Paul's conversion occurred much later, or that he had no contact with pre-resurrection eyewitnesses, would falsify.

atoms.name: Paul verified the gospel with Peter and James (Gal 1-2)
atoms.statementTechnical: Paul visited Jerusalem ~3 years post-conversion (Gal 1:18) spending 15 days with Peter and James, and again 14 years later (Gal 2:2,9) where the pillars added nothing to his gospel and gave the right hand of fellowship.
atoms.statementPlain: Paul checked his gospel with Peter and James, the eyewitnesses, and they confirmed it.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Demonstration that Galatians is late/inauthentic, or that Paul's Jerusalem visits did not involve gospel verification with eyewitnesses, would falsify.

atoms.name: Early eyewitness chain rules out 'telephone tag' myth
atoms.statementTechnical: The 2-6 year chain from cross to Paul's verified contact with Peter and James precludes legendary development ('telephone tag'), since myths require far longer transmission.
atoms.statementPlain: The data is too early for the story to be a garbled myth.
atoms.falsificationCondition: A demonstrated case of a comparable myth forming within 2-6 years among multiple living eyewitnesses would falsify.
atoms.notes: Habermas rejects 'too early to be myth' as a slogan but defends the underlying chronology.

atoms.name: Gospels are Greco-Roman biographies
atoms.statementTechnical: Following a University of London doctoral dissertation, the majority critical view now classifies the Gospels as Greco-Roman bios, i.e., historiographical work.
atoms.statementPlain: Scholars now agree the Gospels are biographies, not a special Holy Spirit genre.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Scholarly consensus reverting to non-biographical genre classification would falsify.

atoms.name: Most doubt is emotional, not factual
atoms.statementTechnical: Clinical-psychological testing of Christians' doubts shows the great majority are emotional rather than factual, characterized by 'what if' questions and affective pain, and are not resolved by evidence.
atoms.statementPlain: Most doubt isn't about facts; it's emotional, and data won't fix it.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Psychological data showing most religious doubt is evidence-driven and resolved by evidence would falsify.
atoms.notes: Habermas cites co-work with a clinical psychologist.

atoms.name: 80% of early creedal material centers on death and resurrection
atoms.statementTechnical: Approximately 80% of the homologia and creedal material in the New Testament concerns Jesus' death and resurrection, indicating divine prioritization of the gospel core.
atoms.statementPlain: Most of the earliest Christian statements are about Jesus' death and resurrection.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Content analysis showing creedal material predominantly addresses other topics would falsify.

atoms.name: Post-salvation works determine eternal capacity for reward
atoms.statementTechnical: Good works do not save, but post-salvation labor in the Lord is not in vain and determines the capacity of eternal enjoyment (1 Cor 15:58).
atoms.statementPlain: Works don't save you, but what you do after salvation shapes your eternity.
atoms.falsificationCondition: Scriptural or theological demonstration that post-salvation works have no bearing on eternal reward would falsify.

atoms.name: Alexander the Great source gap (~300-450 yrs)
atoms.statementTechnical: Earliest source for Alexander is ~300 years after his death; best sources (Arrian, Plutarch) 425-450 years later.
atoms.statementPlain: We trust Alexander sources written centuries later but doubt Gospels written decades later.

atoms.name: Buddhist scriptures 600-800 years after Buddha
atoms.statementTechnical: A PhD Buddhist scholar concedes Buddhist sources date 600-800 years after Buddha's death, with no chain of Lord/disciple sources comparable to Christianity's.
atoms.statementPlain: Buddhist texts are far later than the Gospels.

atoms.name: Audience recall of 65-year-old events
atoms.statementTechnical: Audience poll shows many clearly recall eyewitness events from 65+ years prior, undercutting the claim that John's late date destroys reliability.
atoms.statementPlain: People really do remember things from 65 years ago.

atoms.name: Critical dating of NT documents
atoms.statementTechnical: Critical (including non-Christian) scholars date Mark ~70, Matthew ~80, Luke ~85, John ~90-95, 1 Thessalonians ~50, Paul's epistles 50-60.
atoms.statementPlain: Even skeptical scholars date the sources early.

atoms.name: Telephone-tag / myth objection
atoms.statementTechnical: If the gospel message were garbled transmission over decades, the resurrection data would be unreliable.

atoms.name: Jesus mythicism
atoms.statementTechnical: If Jesus never lived, all resurrection claims collapse.
atoms.notes: Habermas notes only two accredited scholars hold this; Ehrman wrote against it.

atoms.name: 'Christianity is too easy — just believe'
atoms.statementTechnical: Objection that salvation by belief alone is trivial; Habermas replies that NT 'believe' (pisteuo) means trust/surrender, like marriage vows.

atoms.name: 'If the data is so good, why don't critics believe?'
atoms.statementTechnical: Habermas answers that worldview commitments, not data, drive most disbelief.

atoms.name: Pharisaic historiographical method behind Paul's verification
atoms.statementTechnical: Josephus documents Pharisaic teaching-by-repetition and historical transmission; Paul, a Pharisee, applied this method in questioning Peter and James (historesai).
atoms.statementPlain: Paul checked the facts the way Pharisees were trained to.

atoms.name: Eight critical-accepted lines of evidence
atoms.statementTechnical: Eight separate lines of evidence from cross to end of Paul's epistles are accepted by critical scholars; four presented here.

atoms.name: God uses wounded lives
atoms.statementTechnical: Peter, James, and Paul each failed grievously yet were commissioned; application: God uses wounded lives.

atoms.name: Unclassified closing exhortation material
atoms.statementPlain: Exhortation on steadfastness, reward, and Christ's victory over death (1 Cor 15:55-58).
atoms.notes: Devotional close; not a discrete falsifiable claim.

stories.paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 003 - Remarkably Early Historical Information for the Resurrection of Jesus - Gary Habermas

stories.title_or_label: Marriage Vows as the Meaning of 'Believe'
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas's own wedding ceremony; he explains that his first wife died of stomach cancer in 1995 and he later remarried a family friend.
stories.plot_or_sequence: At the wedding, the pastor tells Gary he is about to give away everything he owns. During the vows, his wife stops and emphatically says 'Yes.' Habermas uses this to explain that New Testament 'believe' (pisteuo) means trust, surrender, and self-giving, like saying 'I do' in marriage.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Warm, personal, humorous (audience laughter); leverages the gravity of marriage commitment to elevate the meaning of faith.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That 'believe' in the NT can carry the sense of total trust and surrender, analogous to marital vows.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That pisteuo lexically or contextually must mean this in every NT occurrence; nor that salvation is by works.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Lexical evidence that NT 'believe' never carries the sense of trust/surrender, or that Habermas's anecdote misrepresents the wedding event.

stories.notes: Personal anecdote used to defuse the 'Christianity is too easy' objection; not load-bearing for the resurrection argument.

stories.title_or_label: Audience Poll: Remembering Events 65+ Years Ago
stories.setting_or_context: Live lecture; Habermas asks how many in the audience clearly recall an eyewitness event from 65 or more years ago.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas asks for a show of hands; many hands go up. He says he would not want to call them liars, yet critics dismiss John's Gospel (dated +65) on the grounds that no one remembers that far back.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Interactive, mildly confrontational; uses audience participation to create a lived counterexample.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That some people can and do recall events from 65+ years ago.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That such memories are reliable in detail, that the Gospel traditions were transmitted with comparable fidelity, or that the resurrection appearances were remembered accurately.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the raised hands were mistaken, or that long-term eyewitness memory is systematically unreliable for the relevant kind of event.

stories.notes: Rhetorical counterexample to the 'too late to remember' objection; does not by itself establish the reliability of the Gospel traditions.

stories.setting_or_context: Comparison of ancient historiographical source gaps.
stories.plot_or_sequence: The earliest source for Alexander the Great comes almost 300 years after his death; the two best sources, Arrian and Plutarch, come 425 and 450 years later. Yet historians consider the Alexander sources good. By contrast, critics dismiss John at +60 or Mark at +40.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Argument by comparative absurdity; highlights alleged critical inconsistency.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That historians sometimes accept late sources for other ancient figures.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the Gospels are therefore reliable, or that the standards for Alexander and for a resurrection claim are equivalent.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the Alexander source gap is much smaller than stated, or that historians do not in fact treat those sources as reliable.

stories.notes: Comparative illustration; the underlying historical claim (A11) is an evidence atom, but the rhetorical force is analogical.

characters_or_agents: the PhD Buddhist author of The Buddhist Scriptures
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas cites a book on his shelf by a PhD Buddhist scholar.
stories.plot_or_sequence: The Buddhist author concedes that Christians have the words of their Lord, of the disciples, and of the disciples' disciples, while Buddhists do not; the best Buddhist sources date 600-800 years after Buddha's death.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Appeal to a non-Christian authority conceding Christian advantage.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That some Buddhist scriptures are dated much later than the NT documents.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the NT documents are therefore historically reliable or that the resurrection occurred.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the cited Buddhist sources are earlier than claimed, or that the author's concession is misrepresented.

stories.notes: Comparative illustration; relies on a quoted authority rather than independent argument.

stories.title_or_label: Sunflower Seed and Shell: Homologia and Creeds
stories.setting_or_context: Explanation of the relationship between the earliest gospel message (homologia) and the early creeds.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Picture a sunflower seed: the kernel is the homologia (the earliest agreed-upon message of Jesus' death and resurrection); the shell is the creed that encapsulates it for memorization and transmission. Some people eat the shell too, but most go for the kernel.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Concrete, homely imagery; makes an abstract historiographical distinction memorable.

boundaries.what_it_shows: A conceptual model for how early Christian preaching was packaged into memorizable creedal statements.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the creeds accurately preserve the homologia, or that the homologia is historically true.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the creeds were not early, not memorizable, or not derived from the earliest preaching.

stories.notes: Pedagogical metaphor; the underlying claims are A02 and A03.

stories.title_or_label: Telephone Tag / Misconstrued Message at Dinner
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas illustrates how quickly a message can be garbled.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas imagines having dinner with someone named Bob, misunderstanding that Bob's father died, and then telling a third party. Bob is not present to correct it. In five minutes, the message is misconstrued. Habermas uses this to show that 'telephone tag' can happen quickly, but then argues that Paul's verification with Peter and James rules out telephone tag for the resurrection message.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Self-deprecating humor ('I'm practically deaf'); sets up the need for the eyewitness verification argument.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That oral transmission can be garbled quickly under some conditions.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the early Christian transmission was in fact garbled, or that Paul's verification fully eliminates the possibility of distortion.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Paul's meeting with Peter and James did not function as a verification of the resurrection message, or that early Christian transmission was uncontrolled.

stories.notes: Hypothetical illustration used to frame the 'telephone tag' objection before answering it with Galatians 1-2.

stories.title_or_label: Paul Questions Peter and James: 'Tell Me What You Saw'
stories.setting_or_context: Jerusalem, approximately 3-6 years after the crucifixion (Galatians 1:18), and again 14 years later (Galatians 2:2).
stories.plot_or_sequence: Paul, formerly a persecutor who stood at Stephen's killing, is converted 2-3 years after the cross. Three years later he goes to Jerusalem and spends 15 days with Peter and James. Habermas imagines Paul saying: 'Tell me what you saw on Easter Sunday morning, and I'll tell you what I saw on the road to Damascus.' Paul uses the Greek word historesai (to check out, investigate, question). Fourteen years later Paul returns and presents his gospel to the 'pillars'—Peter, James, and John—to see if he had run in vain. They added nothing to him and gave him the right hand of fellowship.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Dramatic reconstruction; positions Paul as a careful researcher and the Jerusalem leaders as eyewitness verifiers.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Paul reports visiting Peter and James and later checking his gospel with the Jerusalem leaders (Gal 1-2).
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the content of their conversation was specifically about resurrection appearances, or that their agreement guarantees the resurrection occurred.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that Galatians 1-2 does not describe a verification of the gospel, or that the visits did not involve Peter and James.

stories.notes: Structurally load-bearing: this narrative is the core of Habermas's fourth argument against 'telephone tag.' The imagined dialogue is explicitly a reconstruction, not a quotation.

stories.title_or_label: God Uses Wounded Lives: Peter, James, and Paul
stories.setting_or_context: Application point within the lecture, imagining the conversation between Paul, Peter, and James.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas imagines Paul saying to Peter and James: all three of us have been losers. Peter denied the Savior three times; James grew up with Jesus and likely resented him; Paul killed people. Yet all three were commissioned. The practical conclusion: God uses wounded lives and huge ministries.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Pastoral, encouraging; uses the failures of the three leaders to offer hope.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That the NT depicts Peter, James, and Paul as having significant failures before being used by God.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That this pattern is universal, or that it provides evidence for the resurrection.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that the NT does not depict these figures as having failed, or that their commissioning did not follow failure.

stories.notes: Application/exhortation; separable from the historical argument.

stories.title_or_label: Emotional Doubters and the 'What If' Spiral
stories.setting_or_context: Habermas's research on doubt, including a psychological battery of tests administered with a clinical psychologist.
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas says most doubts are emotional, not factual. Emotional doubters ask 'What if?' questions with no evidence and are not helped by more data. He cites C. S. Lewis's line about telling your emotions where to get off. His wife jokes that women doubt more but at least know they're emotional, while men turn over the wrong rocks thinking it's a fact.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Humorous, pastoral; uses gender stereotype humor to make a point about the nature of doubt.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That Habermas and a psychologist found many doubts to be emotional rather than factual.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That all doubt is emotional, or that factual evidence is irrelevant to all doubters.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that most doubt is in fact driven by factual concerns, or that the psychological battery did not support the conclusion.

stories.notes: Illustrates the distinction between factual and emotional doubt; supports the claim that data alone will not resolve most doubt.

stories.title_or_label: Boiling a Frog Slowly: The Deceitfulness of Sin
stories.plot_or_sequence: Habermas cites the old saying that a frog placed in water will not jump out as the water heats slowly. He uses this to illustrate Hebrews' warning not to be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Cautionary; uses a familiar folk image to warn against gradual spiritual drift.

boundaries.what_it_shows: A memorable image of gradual hardening.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the frog anecdote is biologically accurate, or that spiritual hardening works exactly like the metaphor.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that frogs do jump out of slowly heated water (the anecdote is scientifically dubious).

stories.notes: Folk illustration; not load-bearing for any historical claim.

stories.title_or_label: Paul Trash-Talking Death and the Devil
stories.plot_or_sequence: Paul quotes the Old Testament: 'Death, where is your sting? Grave, where is your victory?' Habermas says Paul is not being a poet but is trash-talking death and the devil. Death has been defeated; the empty tomb means the devil has lost his prized possession. Believers can be hurt but cannot be kept. Therefore be steadfast, work, and know that eternal life starts now.
stories.emotional_or_rhetorical_load: Triumphalistic, rousing; the climax of the lecture.

boundaries.what_it_shows: That 1 Corinthians 15 ends with a triumphant exhortation based on the resurrection.
boundaries.what_it_does_not_show: That the resurrection occurred, or that the devil exists as a personal being.
boundaries.what_would_falsify_the_narrative: Evidence that 1 Corinthians 15:55-58 is not about victory over death, or that Paul did not intend it as a taunt.

stories.notes: Exhortational climax; depends on the resurrection claim but does not establish it.

narrative_arc.opening_device: Habermas opens with the bold claim that the resurrection is Christianity's load-bearing claim: 'If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true. You don't have to solve every problem in the Bible.'
narrative_arc.central_tension: Critics dismiss the resurrection as late legend ('telephone tag'), but Habermas argues that the earliest data—homologia, creeds, Paul's conversion, and Paul's verification with Peter and James—are too early for myth.
narrative_arc.resolution_or_payoff: By approximately six years after the cross, the earliest preaching, the creeds, Paul's conversion, and Paul's verification with the eyewitnesses are all in place, ruling out telephone tag and providing early eyewitness evidence.

stories.notes: The lecture is structured as a cumulative historical argument with embedded illustrations and a closing sermon. The most structurally load-bearing story is st-007 (Paul's verification with Peter and James), which is not separable from the argument. The other stories are illustrative, comparative, or exhortational and are separable from the historical case. Historical claims within stories are linked to evidence atoms where the schema provides them; the imagined dialogue in st-007 is explicitly a reconstruction, not a quotation.

core_relation.sentence: The resurrection of Jesus is established as true if and only if the earliest Christian testimony (homologia, creeds, Paul's conversion, and Paul's verification with Peter and James) is both early enough and rooted in eyewitnesses, which together rule out legend or 'telephone tag'.
core_relation.quote: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true. [S006]

core_relation_run2.sentence: The truth of Christianity stands or falls on the historical fact of the resurrection, which is established by early, eyewitness-grounded testimony (homologia, creeds, Paul's conversion, and his Jerusalem verification) that collectively rules out legend or telephone-tag distortion.
core_relation_run2.quote: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true. [S006]

product_test.quote: You get the resurrection of Jesus, as my good buddy Mike Licona says, you get the resurrection, it's game, set, and match. Christianity is true. [S011]
product_test.reason: The argument is structured so that if any one of the four early-evidence pillars (immediate preaching, early creeds, Paul's conversion, Paul's verification with eyewitnesses) is removed or shown to be late/misconstrued, the conclusion of a reliably transmitted resurrection witness collapses entirely, not merely weakens. Habermas explicitly treats the chain as a package: 'How do you know it's not phone tag? ... It rules phone tag out because he got it from the eyewitnesses.' [S412-S413]

slots.plays_role: External negentropy influx: the revelatory act of God raising Jesus, which is the outside source that initiates and sustains the entire chain of testimony.
slots.quote: If Jesus was raised from the dead, Christianity is true. [S006]

slots.plays_role: Alignment: the apostolic church and Paul are aligned with the gospel kernel; the Jerusalem pillars and Paul verify they are on the same page.
slots.quote: I went to see them again, and I gave them the gospel presentation that I was preaching to see if I was running or had run in vain. [S456]

slots.plays_role: Signal fidelity: the transmission of the resurrection message through homologia, creeds, and Paul's testimony without distortion; 'telephone tag' is the noise the argument rules out.
slots.quote: It rules phone tag out because he got it from the eyewitnesses. [S413]

slots.plays_role: Effective entropy: the tendency of oral tradition to decay into myth or misconstrued data, which the early dating and eyewitness links are meant to counteract.
slots.quote: You know how long it takes to make a myth? ... Paul was too early to be myth. Baloney. [S325-S331]

slots.plays_role: Temporal integration: the compressed timeline from the cross to the creeds, Paul's conversion, and the Jerusalem meetings is the central evidence; time is the variable that makes or breaks the case.
slots.quote: How about six? ... How about six four arguments all from eyewitnesses. [S214]

slots.plays_role: Compression: the homologia and creeds are deliberately compressed, memorizable kernels that preserve the gospel for an illiterate audience.
slots.quote: Picture a sunflower seed. The kernel, the part you eat, is the homologia, but now a shell has been put around it. [S276-S277]

slots.plays_role: Phase transition: Paul's conversion on the Damascus road is a discontinuous state change from persecutor to apostle, which the argument treats as a discrete event that validates the creeds.
slots.quote: And then something happened. Boom. He meets Jesus and now magically all the creeds are true. [S296-S297]

slots.plays_role: Superposition: the open question of whether the tradition is reliable or 'telephone tag' is held unresolved until the evidence is examined; the argument aims to collapse it to one outcome.
slots.quote: How do you know we don't have homologia and creeds and Paul's testimony, but it's telephone tag? [S324]

slots.plays_role: Non-local correlation: the early church in Jerusalem, Paul, Peter, James, and John are correlated witnesses whose independent testimonies converge; the 'right people, right place, right time' convergence.
slots.quote: The earliest ones came out of Jerusalem, right place, within 1 to 2 years after the cross, right time, possibly or probably came from the apostles, right people, and Paul probably knew all of them. [S292]

slots.plays_role: Integration: Paul functions as the local integrator who gathers the homologia, creeds, and eyewitness testimony into a verified gospel, checking it with the pillars.
slots.quote: He goes to Jerusalem plus six, talks to James and Peter and questions them. [S441]

master_equation.one_line: Habermas's argument is best read as a multiplicative evidential chain where early testimony, eyewitness verification, and compressed creeds must all hold together for the resurrection conclusion to stand, though several master-equation slots are only loosely mapped.
breaks: The paper treats the resurrection event itself (G) as a historical premise rather than a negentropy influx that must be sustained; the analogy to a continuous external source is weak.
The slot Q (superposition) is not a native category; the paper presents the evidence as already resolved, not as an open possibility awaiting actualization.
The paper adds a strong apologetic/polemical factor (defeating skeptical alternatives) that has no slot in the master equation; this is an extra dimension not captured by the product.
The emotional-doubt discussion at the end introduces a psychological factor (emotional vs. factual doubt) that is entirely outside the master-equation slots.
The paper's argument is primarily evidential and historical, not a formal multiplicative law; the 'product' is rhetorical/conditional rather than mathematical.
Slot Q (superposition) is only weakly present: the paper treats the resurrection as a past fact to be established, not as an unresolved possibility held open until actualization.
Slot G is treated as a revelatory act rather than a measurable external negentropy source; the analogy is theological rather than physical.
The paper adds an 'emotional vs. factual doubt' distinction [S561, S571] that has no slot in the master equation.
The paper's '80% of creeds center on the gospel' [S606] is an extra quantitative factor not represented in the ten slots.
extra_factors: The distinction between factual and emotional doubt, and the claim that most doubts are emotional, which functions as a separate explanatory layer.
The pastoral application (be steadfast, labor not in vain) which is not part of the evidential product but is the paper's stated conclusion.

coherence.paper_uuid: Gary Habermas - Chapter 003 - Remarkably Early Historical Information for the Resurrection of Jesus - Gary Habermas

overall.summary: The paper presents a largely coherent cumulative case for the resurrection, with minor definitional ambiguities and a few inferential gaps, but no major contradictions.

dimensions.name: internal_consistency
reasons: The central claim that early, eyewitness-based data rules out myth (A06) is consistently supported by the homologia (A02), creeds (A03), Paul's conversion (A04), and verification with Peter and James (A05).

The objection that Christianity is too easy (A17) is addressed by redefining 'believe' as trust/surrender, which aligns with the overall argument that the resurrection is the load-bearing claim (A01).
The claim that most doubt is emotional (A08) is consistent with the later discussion of emotional doubt and the distinction between factual and emotional doubt (S561-S571).
No direct contradictions between atoms were found; the narrative flows logically from early data to verification to application.

dimensions.name: definitional_stability
reasons: Key terms like 'homologia' (A02) and 'creeds' (A03) are defined and used consistently, though the exact relationship between them is clarified via the sunflower seed metaphor (S276-S283).
The term 'believe' is redefined from mere intellectual assent to trust/surrender (A17), which is crucial for the argument but may not be universally accepted.

The concept of 'early' is used flexibly: homologia is immediate, creeds within 1-2 years, Paul's conversion within 2-3 years, and his Jerusalem visit 3 years later (A03, A04, A05). This is generally consistent but could benefit from more precise dating.
The phrase 'critical scholars' is used throughout but not explicitly defined; however, context suggests it refers to non-Christian specialists who accept certain historical facts (S088-S093).

dimensions.name: inferential_connectedness
reasons: The argument that early data rules out myth (A06) is supported by the chain: homologia (A02) -> creeds (A03) -> Paul's conversion (A04) -> verification (A05). Each step is linked to the next.
The inference from Paul's Pharisaic training (A19) to his careful verification (A05) is plausible but relies on an external source (Josephus) and may not be universally accepted.

The claim that 80% of early creedal material centers on death and resurrection (A09) is used to support the centrality of the gospel, but the connection to the overall argument is somewhat tangential.
The leap from historical data to the conclusion that 'Christianity is true' (A01) is a theological inference, not strictly historical, but this is acknowledged as a faith commitment.

dimensions.name: register_boundary_respect
reasons: The paper distinguishes between historical evidence and theological interpretation, e.g., acknowledging that the resurrection is a matter of faith (A01) while presenting historical data.

The use of secular examples (Alexander the Great, Buddhist scriptures) to illustrate the earliness of Christian sources respects the boundary between historical method and theological claim (A11, A12).
The discussion of emotional doubt (A08) moves into psychological territory but is clearly marked as a separate category from factual doubt.
The closing exhortation (A22) shifts to pastoral application, which is appropriate for the genre but does not confuse the historical argument.

tensions.description: The dating of the creeds (within 1-2 years) and Paul's conversion (2-3 years) are close but not identical; the timeline could be seen as slightly overlapping or sequential, but no clear contradiction.
A08 claims most doubt is emotional, while A18 says worldview commitments drive disbelief. These are complementary but could be seen as competing explanations for why people don't believe.

missing_definitions.description: Defined as 'earliest agreed-upon data' (S235), but its exact relationship to creeds and how it was transmitted is not fully specified.
Used frequently but not explicitly defined; context suggests non-Christian specialists who accept certain historical facts, but the criteria for inclusion are unclear.
Used relatively (e.g., 'within 1-2 years', '2-3 years') but no absolute threshold is given for what counts as early enough to rule out myth.

coherence.notes: The paper is a spoken lecture, so some repetition and informal language are expected. The coherence is generally strong, with a clear cumulative argument. The main weaknesses are minor definitional ambiguities and a few inferential leaps that rely on theological assumptions. The score reflects a well-structured presentation that largely avoids internal contradiction.
